claim: Transcriptional assays such as yeast two-hybrid and TANGO convert transient protein-protein interactions into stable expression of transgenes.
source: Transcriptional assays, such as yeast two-hybrid and TANGO, that convert transient protein-protein interactions (PPIs) into stable expression of transgenes are powerful tools for PPI discovery, screens, and analysis of cell populations.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known property of these assays.

claim: SPARK requires both a PPI to deliver a protease proximal to its cleavage peptide and blue light to uncage the cleavage site for proteolytic release of a membrane-tethered transcription factor.
source: We have developed SPARK (Specific Protein Association tool giving transcriptional Readout with rapid Kinetics), in which proteolytic release of a membrane-tethered transcription factor (TF) requires both a PPI to deliver a protease proximal to its cleavage peptide and blue light to uncage the cleavage site.
evidence: This describes the design principle of SPARK as stated in the abstract.

claim: SPARK was used to detect 12 different PPIs in mammalian cells.

claim: SPARK has three components: a transcription factor tethered to protein interaction partner 'A' and to the plasma membrane via a protease cleavage site; a protease fused to protein interaction partner 'B'; and a reporter gene.
source: As shown in Figure 1A–B, SPARK has three components: a transcription factor (TF) that is tethered to protein interaction partner 'A' as well as to the plasma membrane (or other intracellular membrane, sequestered from the nucleus) via a protease cleavage site ('TEVcs' for tobacco etch virus protease cleavage site); a protease ('TEVp' for tobacco etch virus protease) that is fused to protein interaction partner 'B'; and a reporter gene whose transcription is triggered by TF translocation to the nucleus.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: TF release from the plasma membrane via TEVcs cleavage requires the coincidence of protein A-protein B interaction and externally-applied blue light.
source: TF release from the plasma membrane via TEVcs cleavage requires the coincidence of two events: protein A-protein B interaction and externally-applied blue light.
evidence: This is stated as a design principle of SPARK.

claim: The TEVp protease is tuned to have low affinity for its TEVcs substrate and cleavage is only significant when the two are brought into proximity via A-B interaction.

claim: The TEVcs is caged by an evolved LOV domain (eLOV) which was generated by directed evolution to tightly cage the TEVcs sequence and prevent its cleavage in the dark state.
source: Second, the TEVcs is caged by an 'evolved LOV domain' (eLOV), which we previously generated by directed evolution to tightly cage the TEVcs sequence and prevent its cleavage in the dark state (Wang et al., 2017).

claim: A brief (<1 s) pulse of 467 nm light alters the eLOV protein conformation, unblocking the adjacent TEVcs and allowing cleavage.

evidence: This is stated as a property of eLOV.

claim: After ~100 s without blue light, eLOV spontaneously reverts to its dark state conformation and again blocks TEVcs.
source: After ~100 s without blue light, eLOV spontaneously reverts to its dark state conformation and again blocks TEVcs.
evidence: This is stated as a property of eLOV.

claim: The β2-adrenergic receptor (β2AR) is a 7-transmembrane GPCR that recruits the soluble cytosolic effector protein β-arrestin2 after stimulation with small-molecule agonist isoproterenol.
source: To test the SPARK design with a well-established cellular PPI, we selected the β2-adrenergic receptor (β2AR), a 7-transmembrane GPCR that recruits the soluble cytosolic effector protein β-arrestin2 after stimulation with small-molecule agonist isoproterenol.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about β2AR.

claim: HEK293T cells expressing β2AR-β-arrestin2 SPARK components stimulated for 5 min with both 467 nm light (60 mW/cm2) and isoproterenol showed robust Citrine expression 9 hours after stimulation.
source: HEK293T cells expressing these SPARK components were stimulated for 5 min with both 467 nm light (60 mW/cm2) and isoproterenol. Under these conditions, we expect SPARK components to interact and release the transcription factor, Gal4, from the plasma membrane. Consequently, we should observe transcription and translation of the Citrine fluorescent protein reporter gene. Nine hours after stimulation of the HEK cells, we fixed them and imaged Citrine expression. Figure 1C shows robust Citrine expression in the light- and isoproterenol-treated cells.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: HEK293T cells expressing β2AR-β-arrestin2 SPARK components showed negligible Citrine expression in light-only or isoproterenol-only conditions.
source: Essential for a functional 'AND' gate, we detected negligible Citrine expression in the light-only or isoproterenol-only cells.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: SPARK with UAS-luciferase reporter showed a robust increase in luciferase expression in light- and isoproterenol-treated cells compared to light-only or isoproterenol-only cells.
source: By repeating the above experiment, but replacing the UAS-Citrine gene with a UAS-luciferase gene, and quantifying luminescence on a platereader, we again detected a robust increase in reporter gene transcription in light- and isoproterenol-treated cells compared to light-only or isoproterenol-only cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: TEVcs with P1´=M displayed the highest signal and strongest proximity dependence in the context of β2AR-β-arrestin2 SPARK.
source: Figure 1—figure supplement 1A shows that P1´=M displayed the highest signal and strongest proximity dependence in the context of β2AR-β-arrestin2 SPARK, and hence we selected this TEVcs sequence for all subsequent experiments in this study.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: With short stimulation times or low SPARK component expression levels, eLOV is the best light gate because it gives the highest signal in the +light condition.

evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and E.

claim: When SPARK components are highly overexpressed and the stimulation time is increased from 5 min to 15 min, hLOV1 is the best light gate because it gives the lowest signal in the no-light condition.
source: When SPARK components are highly overexpressed, and the stimulation time is increased from 5 min to 15 min, however, hLOV1 is the best light gate, because it gives the lowest signal in the no-light condition (i.e., best steric protection of TEVcs in the dark state, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).

claim: The mismatched SPARK pairs β2AR-calmodulin and MK2-β-arrestin2 fail to drive Citrine expression.
source: To test SPARK-PPI specificity, we replaced one protein partner in the β2AR-β-arrestin2 SPARK pair with a non-interacting protein. Figure 1E shows that the mismatched pairs β2AR-calmodulin and MK2-β-arrestin2 fail to drive Citrine expression.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: SPARK is not activated merely by recruitment of TEVp to the vicinity of TEVcs without direct complexation mediated by the A-B PPI.
source: We wondered whether mere recruitment of TEVp to the vicinity of TEVcs, without direct complexation mediated by the A-B PPI, would be sufficient to give proteolytic cleavage and TF release. To test this, we generated a mismatched SPARK pair using β-arrestin2 (protein B) and the transmembrane domain of CD4 (protein A). We transfected HEK cells with these SPARK constructs along with a V5-tagged β2AR expression plasmid. We then drove arrestin-TEVp translocation from the cytosol to the plasma membrane by addition of isoproterenol (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A). Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B show that, even when arrestin-TEVp is recruited to the immediate vicinity of the TM (CD4) SPARK TF component, no SPARK activation (citrine expression) is observed.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: SPARK is a very specific detector of direct A-B interaction.
source: This demonstrates that SPARK is a very specific detector of direct A-B interaction, and is not activated merely by A-B proximity.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the proximity experiment.

claim: 30% of total TEVcs is cleaved after 5 min of light and isoproterenol stimulation in β2AR-β-arrestin2 SPARK.

claim: The cleavage yield of TEVcs increases to 48% after 30 min of light and isoproterenol stimulation in β2AR-β-arrestin2 SPARK.

claim: SPARK can be stimulated equipotently by ordinary room light or blue LED.

Figure 1—figure supplement 2D shows that the signal ratios obtained are the same whether the light source is a blue LED or ambient room light.
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: All 12 PPI pairs tested with SPARK worked on the first try without any optimization of geometries or linkers.

Importantly, these results were all obtained simply by cloning protein-coding genes into positions A and B of the constructs in Figure 1A. We did not vary geometries or linkers or create panels of constructs to test for each PPI of interest. The success of all 12 PPI pairs on the first try demonstrates that the SPARK scaffold is robust and highly modular in its design.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the generality testing results.

claim: The success of all 12 PPI pairs on the first try demonstrates that the SPARK scaffold is robust and highly modular in its design.
source: The success of all 12 PPI pairs on the first try demonstrates that the SPARK scaffold is robust and highly modular in its design.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the generality testing.

claim: A light window that overlaps with the peak of A-B interaction will result in SPARK activation and gene transcription.
source: For instance, if an A-B PPI has the time course shown in Figure 3A, left, a light window that overlaps with the peak of A-B interaction will result in SPARK activation and gene transcription, whereas a light window that is right-shifted to a later time period (Figure 3A, right) will not.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: A light window that is right-shifted to a later time period after A-B interaction has ended will not result in SPARK activation.
source: For instance, if an A-B PPI has the time course shown in Figure 3A, left, a light window that overlaps with the peak of A-B interaction will result in SPARK activation and gene transcription, whereas a light window that is right-shifted to a later time period (Figure 3A, right) will not.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: The β2AR-β-arrestin2 interaction extent is high in the initial time period (0–5 min) and then falls off rapidly in the 5–10 min range.
source: To test this concept, we used the β2AR-arrestin2 SPARK constructs, applied isoproterenol at t = 0, and read out luciferase expression after shifting the light window to various time ranges (e.g., 0–5 min, 5–10 min, 15–20 min, etc.). Figure 3C shows that the β2AR-β-arrestin2 interaction extent is high in the initial time period (0–5 min), and then falls off rapidly in the 5–10 min range.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The β2AR-arrestin interaction peaks between 1–3 minutes and then falls off.
source: This is consistent with previous reports showing that the β2AR-arrestin interaction peaks between 1–3 minutes and then falls off (Reiner et al., 2010; Eichel et al., 2016; Lobingier et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to published work.

claim: Isoproterenol and isoetharine are both full agonists of β2AR.
source: Isoproterenol and isoetharine are both full agonists, while clenbuterol is a partial agonist, evoking a weaker downstream response and kinetically slower recruitment of arrestin (Kaya et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: Clenbuterol is a partial agonist of β2AR, evoking a weaker downstream response and kinetically slower recruitment of arrestin.
source: Isoproterenol and isoetharine are both full agonists, while clenbuterol is a partial agonist, evoking a weaker downstream response and kinetically slower recruitment of arrestin (Kaya et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citation to published work.

claim: Carvedilol is an inverse agonist of β2AR, which can attenuate downstream signaling while still recruiting arrestin, albeit more weakly than a full agonist.
source: Carvedilol is an inverse agonist, which can attenuate downstream signaling while still recruiting arrestin, albeit more weakly than a full agonist (Wisler et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citation to published work.

claim: The full agonists isoproterenol and isoetharine evoked strong responses (maximum ±ligand signal ratios ~18) and transient arrestin association.
source: We used the light staggering scheme in Figure 3A to examine the temporal response of the β2AR-arrestin2 interaction to these different ligands. As expected, the full agonists isoproterenol and isoetharine evoked strong responses (maximum ±ligand signal ratios ~18) and transient arrestin association.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: Clenbuterol induced a much smaller response and delayed onset of arrestin recruitment.
source: Clenbuterol induced a much smaller response and delayed onset of arrestin recruitment, consistent with its classification as a partial agonist.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: Carvedilol produced a delayed but sustained interaction with β-arrestin2.
source: Interestingly, carvedilol produced a delayed but sustained interaction with β-arrestin2.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: Two Class A GPCRs, β2AR and DRD1, give strong SPARK responses within 5 min of ligand addition but much lower SPARK-driven luciferase expression shortly after ligand washout.
source: Figure 3D shows that two Class A GPCRs, β2AR and DRD1, give strong SPARK responses within 5 min of ligand addition but much lower SPARK-driven luciferase expression shortly after ligand washout.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Class A GPCRs interact weakly and transiently with arrestin.
source: This is consistent with previous studies showing that Class A GPCRs interact weakly and transiently with arrestin (Oakley et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated with citation to published work.

claim: The Class B GPCR AVPR2 recruits arrestin quickly and maintains a strong interaction with arrestin even 90 min after washout of the ligand vasopressin.
source: In contrast, the Class B GPCR AVPR2 recruits arrestin quickly and maintains a strong interaction with arrestin even 90 min after washout of the ligand vasopressin.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: DRD2 is a Class A GPCR due to its transient association with arrestin.
source: The dopamine receptor DRD2 has not previously been classified as type A or B, but our data in Figure 3D strongly suggest that it is Class A, like DRD1, due to its transient association with arrestin.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from SPARK data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: SPARK can resolve PPI dynamics with a temporal resolution of 5 min via a single timepoint readout.
source: We conclude that, due to its time-gated transcriptional design, SPARK can resolve PPI dynamics, with a temporal resolution of 5 min, via a single timepoint readout that is simple and scalable (our assays in Figure 3 were performed in 96-well plate format).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the time course experiments.

claim: SPARK enabled classification of DRD2 as a Class A-type GPCR.
source: Excitingly, this feature enabled us to classify a receptor (DRD2) important in emotion, cognition, and neurological disease as a Class A-type GPCR.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from SPARK data.

claim: A single round of FACS sorting enriched the matched PPI cell population by 51-fold over the mismatched cell population.
source: We analyzed the resulting cell population by RT-qPCR to determine the ratio of arrestin cells (matched SPARK) to calmodulin cells (mismatched SPARK). Figure 4C shows that a single round of FACS sorting enriched the matched PPI cell population by 51-fold over the mismatched cell population.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The large enrichment factor in a single round of selection suggests that it should be possible to use SPARK to accurately discover PPIs that occur during selected time windows of interest.
source: Such a large enrichment factor in a single round of selection suggests that it should be possible to use SPARK to accurately discover PPIs that occur during selected time windows of interest.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the FACS enrichment experiment.

claim: TANGO requires a vasopressin receptor 2 tail domain (V2 tail) to be fused to the GPCR's C-terminal end to artificially enhance arrestin recruitment and increase TANGO signal.
source: Furthermore, when applied to GPCRs, TANGO requires a vasopressin receptor 2 tail domain (V2 tail) to be fused to the GPCR's C-terminal end, to artificially enhance arrestin recruitment and increase TANGO signal.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement of TANGO.

claim: The ±ligand signal ratio was 16.4-fold higher for SPARK than for TANGO under 15 min light and isoproterenol stimulation conditions.
source: HEK293T cells expressing the respective constructs were treated with light and isoproterenol for 15 min, then cultured for 9 hr, before quantitation of luciferase expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B). The ±ligand signal ratio was 16.4-fold higher for SPARK than for TANGO under these conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: With 18 hr isoproterenol incubation, the TANGO ± ligand signal ratio increased from 1.2 to 1.5, but was still far lower than the SPARK signal ratio of 11.8.
source: Since the TANGO assay is typically performed with much longer periods of ligand stimulation (Barnea et al., 2008; Kroeze et al., 2015), we repeated the assay but increased the isoproterenol incubation to 18 hr (light period was still 15 min for SPARK). The TANGO ± ligand signal ratio increased from 1.2 to 1.5, but was still far lower than the SPARK signal ratio, which was 11.8.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: The main reason for the difference in performance between SPARK and TANGO appears to be high TANGO background in the no-ligand condition.
source: The main reason for this difference in performance appears to be high TANGO background in the no-ligand condition.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the comparison data.

claim: SPARK has much lower no-ligand luciferase expression than TANGO because the eLOV domain protects the TEVcs from cleavage in the dark state.
source: SPARK has much lower no-ligand luciferase expression because the eLOV domain protects the TEVcs from cleavage in the dark state.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for SPARK's lower background.

claim: TANGO's TEVcs is exposed throughout the entire period (hours to days) that the TANGO components are expressed, leading to high accumulated background.
source: In contrast, TANGO's TEVcs is exposed throughout the entire period (hours to days) that the TANGO components are expressed, leading to high accumulated background.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for TANGO's high background.

claim: iTANGO was used to mark neurons exposed to dopamine in the mouse brain.
source: Recently, a light-gated version of TANGO was reported, called iTANGO (Lee et al., 2017). iTANGO was used to mark neurons exposed to dopamine in the mouse brain (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation to published work.

claim: Under all conditions tested, iTANGO gave significantly higher background than SPARK.
source: We found that under all conditions tested, iTANGO gave significantly higher background than SPARK.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: There was 3 to 26-fold greater iTANGO-driven luciferase expression under dark/+ligand and light/no-ligand conditions than SPARK-driven luciferase expression under the same conditions.
source: For example, there was 3 to 26-fold greater iTANGO-driven luciferase expression under dark/+ligand and light/no-ligand conditions, than SPARK-driven luciferase expression under the same conditions.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: SPARK gave 2 to 3-fold greater ±ligand signal ratios compared to iTANGO.
source: This resulted in 2 to 3-fold greater ±ligand signal ratios for SPARK, and 5 to 14-fold greater ±light signal ratios, compared to iTANGO (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: SPARK gave 5 to 14-fold greater ±light signal ratios compared to iTANGO.
source: This resulted in 2 to 3-fold greater ±ligand signal ratios for SPARK, and 5 to 14-fold greater ±light signal ratios, compared to iTANGO (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The high background observed with iTANGO derives mainly from its use of split TEV protease, whose fragments may have high affinity for one another and reverse slowly.
source: We hypothesize that the high background we observed with iTANGO derives mainly from its use of split TEV protease, whose fragments may have high affinity for one another, and reverse slowly, similar to other split proteins (Martell et al., 2016; Kerppola, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis with citations to support the behavior of split proteins.

claim: SPARK signal reverses quickly after ligand washout, whereas iTANGO continues to give signal for 15–45 min longer.
source: To test this possibility, we performed GPCR-arrestin time course assays using both SPARK and iTANGO. Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E show that SPARK signal reverses quickly after ligand washout, whereas iTANGO continues to gives signal for 15–45 min longer.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: iTANGO's design 'traps' PPIs, while SPARK's design is much less perturbative.
source: This is consistent with iTANGO's design 'trapping' PPIs, while SPARK's design is much less perturbative.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the time course data.

claim: SPARK is more sensitive, specific, and accurate than TANGO and iTANGO for PPI detection in cells.
source: Based on our collective observations, we conclude that SPARK is more sensitive, specific, and accurate than TANGO and iTANGO for PPI detection in cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the comparison experiments.

claim: SPARK is highly versatile, able to drive luciferase expression for platereader assays, or fluorescent protein expression for microscopy or FACS-based cell selections.
source: The SPARK assay we have developed converts a specific, transient molecular interaction into a stable and amplifiable reporter gene signal. As such, SPARK is highly versatile, able to drive luciferase expression for platereader assays, or fluorescent protein expression for microscopy or FACS-based cell selections.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of SPARK's capabilities.

claim: It should be facile to couple SPARK to the expression of other reporter genes including APEX for EM and proteomics, antibiotic resistance genes, and various actuators such as opsins and toxins.
source: Though not shown here, it should be facile to couple SPARK to the expression of other reporter genes as well, including APEX for EM (Martell et al., 2012; Lam et al., 2015) and proteomics (Rhee et al., 2013), antibiotic resistance genes, and various actuators such as opsins and toxins.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about future applications with citations to relevant methods.

claim: SPARK is highly specific for direct PPIs and is not activated merely by protein proximity.
source: SPARK is highly specific for direct PPIs, and is not activated merely by protein proximity (e.g., colocalization to the plasma membrane – Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion with reference to Figure 1F.

claim: Only 5 min of light coinciding with a PPI event are sufficient to produce a stable signal that lasts for nine hours to days.
source: We showed that only 5 min of light coinciding with a PPI event are sufficient to produce a stable signal that lasts for nine hours to days.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of SPARK's performance.

claim: When Presto-TANGO was applied to 167 different GPCRs, the majority of them gave signal ratios between 1.3 and 5.
source: SPARK produces much larger signal-to-noise ratios than other PPI assays. When Presto-TANGO was applied to 167 different GPCRs, for example, the majority of them gave signal ratios between 1.3 and 5 (Ref. Kroeze et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation to published work.

claim: SPARK gave signal ratios >15 for five of the eight GPCRs randomly selected.
source: In contrast, SPARK gave signal ratios >15 for five of the eight GPCRs that we randomly selected, and signal ratios >10 for other PPI pairs (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Noise is lower for SPARK than for other assays because the LOV domain prevents proteolytic cleavage outside of the brief light window.
source: The higher signal ratios result from two factors. First, noise is lower for SPARK because the LOV domain prevents proteolytic cleavage outside of the brief light window.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for SPARK's higher signal ratios.

claim: Signal is higher for SPARK than for other assays because the SPARK TEVp-TEVcs pair has higher catalytic turnover (est. 10.8 min−1 for SPARK compared to 0.84 min−1 for TANGO).
source: Second, signal is higher for SPARK because our TEVp-TEVcs pair has higher catalytic turnover (est. 10.8 min−1 for SPARK compared to 0.84 min−1 for TANGO (Kapust et al., 2002); and iTANGO uses split-TEVp (Lee et al., 2017) which is expected to have even slower turnover).
evidence: This is stated with citations to published kinetic data.

claim: iTANGO uses split-TEVp which is expected to have even slower turnover than TANGO.
source: Second, signal is higher for SPARK because our TEVp-TEVcs pair has higher catalytic turnover (est. 10.8 min−1 for SPARK compared to 0.84 min−1 for TANGO (Kapust et al., 2002); and iTANGO uses split-TEVp (Lee et al., 2017) which is expected to have even slower turnover).
evidence: This is stated with citation to published work.

claim: SPARK can be used without artificial enhancement of native affinity (e.g., V2 tail), in contrast to both TANGO and iTANGO.
source: As a result of improved signal ratio, SPARK can be used without artificial enhancement of native affinity (e.g., V2 tail), in contrast to both TANGO and iTANGO.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of SPARK's improved signal ratio.

claim: SPARK can detect the activation of receptors that are opaque to other methods, such as ADRA1A and AGTR2.
source: And due to its higher sensitivity, SPARK can detect the activation of receptors that are opaque to other methods, such as ADRA1A and AGTR2 in Figure 2D, which gave no ±ligand signal difference with Presto-TANGO (Kroeze et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 2D and citation to published work.

claim: FRET gives signal-to-noise ratios of 1.02–1.03 for GPCR-arrestin interactions.
source: FRET is also commonly used to image cellular PPIs, and has been applied to GPCR-arrestin interactions in particular (Nuber et al., 2016). SPARK also gives much larger signal-to-noise ratios than those observed in such FRET experiments (1.02–1.03 S/N in Nuber et al., 2016), partly because SPARK incorporates signal amplification.
evidence: This is stated with citation to published work.

claim: SPARK gives much larger signal-to-noise ratios than FRET experiments, partly because SPARK incorporates signal amplification.
source: FRET is also commonly used to image cellular PPIs, and has been applied to GPCR-arrestin interactions in particular (Nuber et al., 2016). SPARK also gives much larger signal-to-noise ratios than those observed in such FRET experiments (1.02–1.03 S/N in Nuber et al., 2016), partly because SPARK incorporates signal amplification.
evidence: This is stated with citation to published work.

claim: SPARK is more accessible to most laboratories than FRET, as it does not require specialized instrumentation or software as FRET imaging does.
source: SPARK is also more accessible to most laboratories, as it does not require specialized instrumentation or software as FRET imaging does.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of SPARK over FRET.

claim: Irreversible PCAs such as bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC) and split HRP integrate molecular events and produce stable signals.
source: Protein Complementation Assays (PCAs) are another commonly used alternative assay to detect and study cellular PPIs. Irreversible PCAs such as bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC) (Kerppola, 2008) and split HRP (Martell et al., 2016) also integrate molecular events and produce stable signals, but unlike SPARK, they trap PPI partners in an irreversible complex that can perturb cellular signaling and give rise to false positives.
evidence: This is stated with citations to published work.

claim: Irreversible PCAs trap PPI partners in an irreversible complex that can perturb cellular signaling and give rise to false positives.
source: Protein Complementation Assays (PCAs) are another commonly used alternative assay to detect and study cellular PPIs. Irreversible PCAs such as bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC) (Kerppola, 2008) and split HRP (Martell et al., 2016) also integrate molecular events and produce stable signals, but unlike SPARK, they trap PPI partners in an irreversible complex that can perturb cellular signaling and give rise to false positives.
evidence: This is stated with citations to published work.

claim: Reversible PCAs such as split luciferase do not trap but also do not produce stable signals that enable single time point readout or genetic selections as SPARK does.
source: Reversible PCAs such as split luciferase (Ozawa et al., 2001) do not trap, but they also do not produce stable signals that enable single time point readout or genetic selections as SPARK does.
evidence: This is stated with citation to published work.

claim: By integrating through a transcription factor, SPARK is unique in combining a non-trapping design with stable, integrated signal generation.
source: By integrating through a transcription factor, SPARK is unique in combining a non-trapping design with stable, integrated signal generation.
evidence: This is stated as a distinguishing feature of SPARK.

claim: Future applications of SPARK might include examination of GPCR 'biased' signaling.
source: Future applications of SPARK might include examination of GPCR 'biased' signaling (Bologna et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about future applications with citation.

claim: It should be possible to replace the arrestin gene with Gi, Gs, or Gq and compare intensities and time courses of G protein versus arrestin recruitment to GPCRs in response to various ligands.
source: Here, we used only arrestin-TEVp with our GPCR panel, but it should be possible to replace the arrestin gene with Gi, Gs, or Gq and compare intensities and time courses of G protein versus arrestin recruitment to GPCRs in response to various ligands.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about future applications.

claim: SPARK will have utility for PPI discovery and other functional genomics applications.
source: Our model selection using FACS also suggests that SPARK will have utility for PPI discovery and other functional genomics applications.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the FACS selection experiment.

claim: Yeast two hybrid and split ubiquitin assays have been employed for yeast-based selections.
source: Notably, while yeast two hybrid and split ubiquitin assays have been employed for yeast-based selections (Fetchko and Stagljar, 2004; Ito et al., 2001), we are not aware of any applications of these platforms or related ones to mammalian cell-based selections, perhaps because the signal-to-noise ratios of these assays are not sufficiently high to enable selection in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is stated with citations to published work.

claim: The signal-to-noise ratios of yeast two hybrid and split ubiquitin assays may not be sufficiently high to enable selection in mammalian cells.
source: Notably, while yeast two hybrid and split ubiquitin assays have been employed for yeast-based selections (Fetchko and Stagljar, 2004; Ito et al., 2001), we are not aware of any applications of these platforms or related ones to mammalian cell-based selections, perhaps because the signal-to-noise ratios of these assays are not sufficiently high to enable selection in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation with citations to published work.
